articles.headline: Gemini can now read your Google Wallet and chart your spending, but it can't move money
articles.excerpt: US Gemini users can connect Google Wallet and tag it in chat to get budgets, subscription checks and cash-flow charts.
summary: Google has added Google Wallet to the apps that Personal Intelligence in the Gemini app can draw on, alongside Gmail, Photos, YouTube and Search. Every Gemini app user in the US can opt in, on web, Android and iOS, and can also link bank and credit card accounts through Plaid. Google's examples include cash-flow and budget charts, spotting forgotten or price-hiked subscriptions, and planning a holiday budget from last year's spending.

Users switch the connection on under Connected Apps in Personal Intelligence settings and call it up by typing @Google Wallet in a chat; charts render inside the conversation thread. Google stresses that Gemini only gets read access and cannot move, manage or invest money, and the connection can be turned off at any time. A Memory Summary view lets people review, edit or delete the preferences and goals Gemini has stored about them.
articles.whyItMatters: It is a clean template for connecting an assistant to sensitive data: explicit opt-in per source, @-mention invocation, read-only scope stated up front, and a visible memory page users can edit.
articles.imageAlt: A 'Personal Intelligence' pill with the Gemini spark, surrounded by Gmail, Photos, YouTube, Google and Google Wallet app icons

articles.headline: Decision theatre or decision design? Why an AI approval button only counts if real judgment sits behind it
articles.excerpt: Patrizia Bertini argues that human sign-off on AI output is often theatre, and lists what a reviewer needs for it to be a real decision.
summary: Writing in UX Collective, Patrizia Bertini argues that AI has made information cheap but decisions no easier. She cites a BetterUp Labs and Stanford survey in which 40% of US desk workers had received 'workslop' in the past month, costing about two hours each to deal with, and uses the data-information-knowledge-wisdom pyramid to argue that more AI-generated know-how does not add up to judgment. Because a system cannot be held accountable, she says, people are becoming AI supervisors who own the decisions.

The core of the piece contrasts two versions of the same Approve button, using a caseworker reviewing AI-flagged benefit claims. In decision theatre the reviewer gets only a risk score, has no authority to overrule without a manager, no time to look and no way to send feedback. In decision design the reviewer sees the evidence and the model's confidence, can override freely, gets fewer cases with the most uncertain first, and each override is explained and fed back to the system's owners. She ties this to the EU AI Act's human-oversight duty.
articles.whyItMatters: Audit every human-in-the-loop approval for four things: visible evidence and confidence, the authority to override, time to review (uncertain items first), and a feedback path for overrides.
articles.author: Patrizia Bertini
articles.imageAlt: Side-by-side diagram of two identical Approve buttons: 'decision theatre' with no feedback, authority, evidence or time, versus 'decision design' with all four

articles.headline: SAP's design chief: cost is now a design material, so show what an agent task will cost before the click
articles.excerpt: Arin Bhowmick lays out patterns for credit- and usage-priced AI products, from cost estimates on buttons to caps per task.
summary: Arin Bhowmick, chief design officer at SAP, writing personally in UX Collective, argues that the era of flat-rate AI is ending: as products move to credit and usage pricing, every agent action has a price, and showing it is a design job. He points to GitHub Copilot's June 2026 move to usage-based AI Credits, after which developers reported burning large parts of a monthly allowance in hours with no way to predict the cost of a request.

His baseline patterns are: put the cost estimate next to the button, confirm before expensive tasks, show what each task cost (as Replit does per checkpoint), warn early so nobody is cut off mid-task (Claude Enterprise alerts admins at 75% and 90%), and let people cap spend per task or session. He also proposes expressing remaining credits in the user's own units, such as 'enough for about three more prototypes', and asks teams to give each AI feature a cost budget and add cost to design reviews.
articles.whyItMatters: Treat cost like latency or errors in agent flows: show an estimate before a run, confirm big jobs, itemize spend per run, and translate remaining credits into units of work people understand.
articles.author: Arin Bhowmick
articles.imageAlt: Illustration of a person at a laptop surrounded by UI cards: a 'Run with AI?' prompt costing about 12 credits, an AI Credits meter with 1,180 left, and a note saying that's enough for about 3 more prototypes

articles.headline: Why AI builders hand you a lookalike of your design system, and the MCP setup that makes them use the real components
articles.excerpt: Christine Vallaure tested Claude Design and other builders, then rebuilt her prototyping around a component manifest and the Storybook MCP.
summary: In the second part of her In-System Design series for UX Collective, Christine Vallaure explains why prototypes from tools such as Lovable, Bolt, v0, Replit and Claude Design keep getting rebuilt by developers. Their 'connect your design system' option reads a team's components and then recreates them, usually on shadcn and Tailwind, so the screen looks right but none of it points at the real code. Testing Claude Design on her own repo, she found the button's props, values and tokens came back correct, yet Base UI, scoped classes and types were replaced by a frozen copy.

Her fix is not a better prompt but two pieces developers can set up: a generated JSON manifest listing every component, property, allowed value and default, and an MCP connection so the agent asks the system what exists instead of guessing. She walks through the Storybook MCP as the quick route (citing Storybook's test showing 27% fewer tokens and almost three times faster runs) and a custom design-system MCP as the richer one, and argues every pipeline should look things up, choose from a closed list, check against the system, render the result and leave the final call to a person.
articles.whyItMatters: Before trusting any AI prototyping tool with a real product, designers can ask it to show which file a component was imported from, which quickly reveals whether it built with the system or redrew it.
articles.author: Christine Vallaure
articles.imageAlt: Logos of Lovable, Bolt, v0, Replit and Claude Design crossed out next to 'Storybook MCP' and 'Design System MCP' with green check marks

articles.headline: In-system design: an agent moves the same prototype from Storybook to Figma and back without redrawing it
articles.excerpt: The last part of Vallaure's series shows an AI agent rebuilding code prototypes from a matching Figma library, and catching bugs on the way.
summary: Christine Vallaure closes her three-part series by connecting both sides: a Storybook prototype built from real components, a published Figma library whose components carry exactly the same names and properties as the code, and an agent (she uses Claude Code with the Figma Console MCP) sitting between them. Asked to send a course sign-up flow to Figma, the agent rebuilt it from library instances as a clickable prototype and left a note listing what it used, what it had to assemble by hand and which gaps it found. Bringing the edited screens back, it reads each instance's component and props rather than layer names.

She argues the canvas still matters because comparing several versions side by side beats refining one, and says the round trip kept surfacing real problems: a 21-pixel height difference that traced back to a stray browser margin in the code, a dialog without a slot that pushed a better flow, and a spacer hack copied three times. Teams without a code setup can still prototype in Figma against the library, and pressing Cmd+Y shows library instances in purple so hand-drawn elements stand out. Her biggest error source was forgetting to accept library updates.
articles.whyItMatters: Matching component names and properties exactly between Figma and code is the cheap prerequisite that lets agents translate designs instead of guessing.
articles.author: Christine Vallaure
articles.imageAlt: Diagram of a Claude agent building the same sign-up page in code and in Figma, with an arrow showing it pushed between Storybook and Figma

articles.headline: Jakob Nielsen: AI makes open-ended research answers cheap to count, so ask more of them
articles.excerpt: Nielsen argues teams should shift surveys and interviews toward open questions now that AI can code every free-form answer.
summary: Jakob Nielsen argues that the old trade-off in user research has changed: closed questions were cheap to analyze but only measure the categories a team thought of, while open questions surface surprises but used to be too costly to code. He cites a University of Vienna-led study where GPT-5.4 inductively coded 903 open survey answers and reached an Adjusted Rand Index of 0.61 with five human coders on codes and 0.54 on themes, which he treats as good enough for AI to join the coding team under human review.

He recommends keeping a fixed closed core for benchmarks, counting coded verbatims with the original quotes attached, counting each respondent once per theme and not ranking problems by frequency alone. For AI-moderated interviews he points to a Penn State study where the bot probed deeper in only 4.9% of turns and offered leading praise, and he proposes banning praise, probing for concrete episodes and piloting with real people. He also warns against synthetic respondents, citing a benevolence bias that grew with model size across 18 models.
articles.whyItMatters: Teams can now afford to read every open comment from a survey or feedback widget, but the codebook and human review decide whether the counts can be trusted.
articles.author: Jakob Nielsen
articles.imageAlt: Illustration titled 'Closed vs. Open Questions' with a radio-button card beside a red microphone and an empty speech bubble

articles.headline: NN/G's journey mapping primer now covers agents as actors and AI as a mapping assistant
articles.excerpt: NN/G's updated Journey Mapping 101 explains how to map journeys that AI agents run, and where AI can speed up making the map.
summary: Nielsen Norman Group refreshed its Journey Mapping 101 article with a new section on AI. It notes that people are no longer the only actors in a journey, since agents can research, buy or resolve issues on someone's behalf, and describes two options: show the agent's actions, obstacles and approval points alongside the person's goals and emotions, or make the agent the primary actor and map the tools it uses and where it needs human help, without thoughts or feelings.

For making the map, Huei-Hsin Wang and Sarah Gibbons suggest using AI to draft a hypothesis map from stakeholder knowledge, tag interview excerpts by stage and lane, cluster support tickets and reviews, turn a static map into an interactive prototype and brainstorm 'how might we' questions. They stress that agent behavior should come from logs and observation, that AI outputs should be checked against quotes and participant IDs, and that much of a map's value comes from the team discussion AI cannot replace.
articles.whyItMatters: As products add agents that act for users, journey maps need a lane for what the agent does and where the person must approve or step in.
articles.author: Huei-Hsin Wang, Sarah Gibbons
articles.imageAlt: Stylized journey map with three colored phases, an emotion curve and speech bubbles with sad, happy and neutral faces

articles.headline: NN/G's research-in-the-loop: build the measurement into each release when AI makes shipping cheap
articles.excerpt: Tony Alicea proposes adding a research section to specs that both people and coding agents read, so each release is instrumented.
summary: Nielsen Norman Group's Tony Alicea argues that AI coding agents have made shipping cheaper than studying, so long pre-build research is harder to justify, but releases only show what users did, not why. His answer is research-in-the-loop: research sets what each release must measure and when to go talk to people. It covers three jobs: evaluation of predicted outcomes, investigation of surprising behavior, and open-ended discovery, which instrumentation cannot replace.

In practice teams add a research section to the plain-language spec that coding agents also read, listing expected outcomes, signs of success and harm, what to track and when to talk to users; a help-desk ticket-transfer example shows how. Qualitative work stays on a regular cadence, is triggered by data anomalies, and comes first for hard-to-reverse calls like pricing. The article flags limits such as causation and off-system workarounds, and lists new skills for researchers, from spec writing to analytics instrumentation.
articles.whyItMatters: Adding success and harm criteria plus tracking requirements to every AI-built feature spec keeps research from being skipped when teams ship weekly.
articles.author: Tony Alicea
articles.imageAlt: NN/G title card with a magnifying glass over a grid of colored dots

articles.headline: Figma Weave's Itay Schiff: decide which creative friction to automate and which to keep
articles.excerpt: On Figma's blog, Weave's co-founder argues AI should take the labor of making, not the thinking that happens inside it.
summary: Itay Schiff, co-founder and chief creative officer of Figma Weave, writes that the question is no longer whether to use AI in creative work but which steps to hand over. He opens with himself reaching for ChatGPT minutes into a writing class he joined to think more clearly, and calls himself a daily AI user who still worries creators give away the parts of the work that matter most to them.

He separates pure labor, such as green-screen cleanup and tracking, from productive friction where ideas form, like trimming a shot or writing a brief. Generation is not authorship: fast outputs look finished, so without shaping everyone gets similar, mediocre work. A Weave campaign needed many rounds on story and styling after a quick first generation. He describes an open mode for exploring and a closed mode for committing to repeatable workflows, and says good tools should let people reopen earlier choices.
articles.whyItMatters: When adding AI to a workflow, map each step as labor or judgment and keep the judgment steps editable and reopenable rather than fully automated.
articles.author: Itay Schiff
articles.imageAlt: Illustration by Jose Flores of a gold woven handbag with blue flowers beside red and orange flowers on a bright yellow background

articles.headline: LangChain raises $300M at a $3B valuation to sell model-neutral agent management
articles.excerpt: CapitalG led the Series C; LangChain says more than 7,000 organizations now use its LangSmith agent platform.
summary: LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation, more than double the $1.25 billion it was valued at about a year ago. CapitalG led the round, with GIC and DFJ Growth joining as significant new investors alongside IVP and Sapphire Ventures; Salesforce Ventures, Insight Partners, QuantumLight and MongoDB Ventures also came in. The company says over 7,000 organizations use LangSmith, including Harvey, Rippling, Clay, NVIDIA, Toyota and Salesforce.

Having started as an open-source library in 2022, LangChain now pitches LangSmith as a model-, cloud- and ecosystem-neutral platform with three parts: an agent runtime (Deep Agents, LangGraph, managed agents, sandboxes, Fleet), agent improvement (observability, evaluation and an agent that proposes fixes) and governance gateways for model budgets, fallbacks and tool access. Customers cite gains like Workday cutting agent deployment from five months to under a day. A launch event is set for November 20.
articles.whyItMatters: Budgets, fallbacks, tool permissions and run traces are becoming standard agent infrastructure, so product UIs will increasingly be expected to surface them to admins and users.
articles.author: Harrison Chase
articles.imageAlt: LangChain announcement card reading '$300M raise at a $3B valuation, led by CapitalG' with Sapphire, IVP, GIC and DFJ Growth logos

articles.headline: Designing Claude: Jenny Wen demos how Anthropic's design team uses Claude to design Claude
articles.excerpt: An hour with Anthropic's design lead on designing for unpredictable AI, agent autonomy and a live demo of her own workflow.
summary: In this Double Diamond episode, Jenny Wen, design lead at Anthropic, shows how she uses Claude in her own design work, including using Cowork to synthesize research and product feedback. The conversation covers how her team designs AI products whose outcomes are unpredictable, what they learn from internal users, how Cowork came together and how to help people understand what an AI can actually do.

Later chapters get into chat versus AI-generated interfaces, balancing agent autonomy with plans and user control, and how to show progress while an agent works, before a live demo of using Claude to design Claude. Wen also talks about how designers and engineers now work together, why craft, execution and shipping count as design skills, and where design tools go next. The channel notes it was recorded in March 2026, so some product details have since changed.
articles.whyItMatters: It is a rare first-hand look at how a frontier lab's designers handle agent plans, progress and control in a shipping product.
articles.author: Jenny Wen
articles.imageAlt: Black-and-white portrait of Jenny Wen on a red background with the text 'Jenny Wen, Design Lead, Anthropic'
